content: The Care for Child Development Guide for Clinical Practice, published by the World Health Organization (WHO), is a comprehensive resource aimed at improving the care provided to young children. It emphasizes the importance of child development, the role of health personnel education, and the delivery of healthcare services. The guide includes teaching materials and practical instructions for clinical sessions, both inpatient and outpatient, to enhance the skills of healthcare providers in supporting child development. Objectives of Clinical Practice The clinical practice component of the course Counsel the Family on Care for Child Development allows participants to apply newly acquired skills with children and their caregivers. The specific objectives include: Identifying the characteristics of caregiver-child interactions. Counseling caregivers on recommended play and communication activities. Observing how children and caregivers respond to these activities. Helping caregivers recognize and appropriately respond to their child’s cues. Assisting caregivers in solving problems related to care at home. Clinical Sessions Overview The clinical sessions are divided into inpatient and outpatient settings, each with distinct objectives and tasks. Inpatient Session: Interacting with a Child The inpatient session occurs on the first day in a hospital’s children’s ward. Participants practice interacting with sick children using play and communication activities. They learn to: Approach a sick child gently to avoid fear. Gain the child’s attention using age-appropriate items. Follow the child’s lead by copying their sounds and gestures. Engage the child in play and communication activities suited to their age and condition. Gradually increase the child’s activity level and encourage the use of new skills. Participants also observe how children respond to these activities and learn to select appropriate activities based on the child’s age and condition. The session highlights the importance of play and communication for hospitalized children, as these activities can prevent developmental delays and contribute to physical recovery. Preparation for the Inpatient Session The clinical instructor must prepare by coordinating with hospital staff, obtaining permission to conduct the session, and selecting appropriate children for participants to work with. Caregivers are informed about the session, and the children’s beds are marked for easy identification. The instructor demonstrates the tasks to be practiced, emphasizing sensitivity and responsiveness to the child’s cues. Outpatient Sessions: Counseling the Caregiver The outpatient sessions take place on the second and third days in settings such as clinics or feeding programs. These sessions focus on counseling caregivers rather than directly interacting with children. Participants: Observe caregiver-child interactions. Ask caregivers about their play and communication practices at home. Use checklists and counseling cards to guide their advice. Coach caregivers in trying new activities and responding to their child’s cues. Help caregivers address challenges in providing care at home. The goal is for participants to work in pairs, counseling three to five caregivers and their children during each session. One participant leads the counseling while the other observes, and both complete a checklist for the session. They demonstrate skills, supervise participants, and provide feedback during debriefing sessions. The instructor must be trained in the course, experienced in teaching child development in clinical settings, and comfortable working with children and caregivers. Preparation includes reviewing session instructions, coordinating with local staff, and ensuring the availability of materials such as toys and counseling cards. Importance of Sensitivity and Responsiveness The guide emphasizes the critical role of sensitivity and responsiveness in caregiving. Sensitivity involves being aware of the child’s signals and interpreting them accurately, while responsiveness requires providing prompt and appropriate reactions to these signals. These skills are foundational for nurturing care and contribute significantly to a child’s healthy development. Participants are encouraged to practice these skills during both inpatient and outpatient sessions. Debriefing and Reflection After each session, participants return to the classroom for debriefing. They discuss their experiences, review the skills practiced, and identify ways to improve. Photos or videos taken during the sessions can be used to illustrate effective caregiving practices. The debriefing also includes a discussion of the most appropriate activities for sick children and how participants demonstrated sensitivity and responsiveness. This guide provides a structured approach to training healthcare providers in supporting child development through practical, hands-on experience in clinical settings. It underscores the importance of play, communication, and caregiver involvement in promoting the well-being and recovery of children.
